reference.source: British Committee for Standards in Haematology acute myeloid leukaemia guidance
clinicalPearls: A medical emergency of symptomatic hyperleucocytosis, most often in acute myeloid leukaemia (especially monocytic and myelomonocytic subtypes) with very high blast counts, or in the blast phase of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia causes leukostasis less readily at any given count because lymphoblasts are smaller and less adhesive than myeloblasts.

The dominant clinical picture is pulmonary (dyspnoea, hypoxia, diffuse infiltrates) and neurological (confusion, headache, visual change, stupor), reflecting microcirculatory obstruction in lung and brain.
Early mortality is high, so urgent cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide and/or prompt induction chemotherapy, together with leucapheresis in selected unstable patients, should not be delayed.
Tumour lysis syndrome and disseminated intravascular coagulation frequently coexist and must be anticipated and managed concurrently.
Red-cell transfusion should be avoided or minimised until the white-cell count is controlled, because it raises whole-blood viscosity and can precipitate clinical deterioration.
Platelet transfusion, in contrast, does not appreciably raise viscosity and may be given to reduce the risk of intracranial haemorrhage.
Beware spurious laboratory results from metabolically active leucocytes: pseudohyperkalaemia, artefactually low arterial oxygen ('leucocyte larceny') and spurious hypoglycaemia.
reference.pathophysiology: A greatly elevated count of large, poorly deformable and adhesive myeloid blasts increases blood viscosity and plugs the microcirculation. Blasts compete with tissues for oxygen, adhere to and damage the endothelium, and release cytokines that promote further leucocyte-endothelial interaction and local hypoxia. The lungs and central nervous system are most vulnerable, producing hypoxaemic respiratory failure and neurological dysfunction; endothelial injury, coagulation activation and concurrent tumour lysis add the risks of haemorrhage, disseminated intravascular coagulation and metabolic derangement.
additionalDifferentials: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with white-cell differential and blast percentage
Blood film for blasts and features of leukaemia
Coagulation screen with fibrinogen and D-dimer for DIC
Urea, electrolytes, urate, phosphate and calcium for tumour lysis
Arterial blood gas (interpreted with awareness of leucocyte artefact)
Chest radiograph and CT head where neurological signs are present
Lactate dehydrogenase and rapid confirmatory bone marrow or immunophenotyping
redFlags: Altered mental status or focal neurological deficit
Rapidly rising blast count with clinical deterioration
reference.prognosis: Leukostasis carries a high risk of early death from respiratory or cerebral complications and intracranial haemorrhage; prompt cytoreduction improves survival. Longer-term outcome is determined by the biology and treatment response of the underlying leukaemia.
pitfalls: Transfusing red cells before cytoreduction and worsening leukostasis
Trusting an artefactually low arterial oxygen tension caused by leucocyte oxygen consumption
Delaying cytoreductive therapy while awaiting definitive diagnosis
Failing to anticipate and manage concurrent tumour lysis syndrome and DIC
Misinterpreting pseudohyperkalaemia and administering unnecessary or harmful treatment
references: British Committee for Standards in Haematology guideline on the management of acute myeloid leukaemia
management: Urgent cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide and prompt induction chemotherapy for the underlying leukaemia
Leucapheresis in selected unstable patients to rapidly lower the circulating blast burden
Anticipate and treat tumour lysis syndrome with vigorous hydration and rasburicase or allopurinol
Manage concurrent disseminated intravascular coagulation with blood-product support
Avoid or minimise red-cell transfusion until the white-cell count is controlled, as it raises whole-blood viscosity
Respiratory support with oxygen and ventilatory assistance, and close neurological monitoring for cerebral involvement
Emergency haematology referral and definitive treatment of the underlying acute myeloid or blast-phase chronic myeloid leukaemia
